https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.title: Iran seized a ship: what Tehran does next matters more
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.text:
Anxieties are running deep. Earlier on Saturday Iranian commandos descending from a helicopter seized a Portuguese-flagged vessel, the MSC Aries, as it passed through the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of the United Arab Emirates. The ship was “linked to Israel”, according to Iranian state media. MSC is affiliated to a company run by Eyal Ofer, the Israeli billionaire.
In capitals around the world there is an expectation that Iran’s next move will be even more consequential as it weighs a response to the Israeli attack on its consulate in Damascus on April 1, which killed seven members of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC), including two generals. There is a growing consensus that Iran will eschew “strategic patience” in favour of striking targets in Israel in retaliation.
Overnight President Biden urged Iran not to mount a direct attack on Israel, but said that he expected it “sooner than later”.
The warning is reminiscent of the intelligence briefings that preceded Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
Airlines, reminded of the accidental shooting down of a Ukrainian passenger jet in 2020, are cancelling flights, while planes that would normally fly over Iranian airspace are being rerouted. India is the latest country to warn its citizens against travel to both Iran and Israel.
Hossein Amir-Abdollahian, the Iranian foreign minister, is meanwhile basking in the sort of limelight that only a crisis can bring, with a string of calls from his counterparts worldwide urging restraint — although as some Iranians have noted with grim humour, he would probably be the last person to be told if an attack was to be launched.
But for all the bombast coming from Iranian officials, there is a striking absence of “war fever” among Iranians themselves, most of whom are more concerned with the economic crisis afflicting their country. Indeed, the level of general apathy towards the regime and its intentions stands in marked contrast with the rising concern internationally.
Most Iranians are preoccupied with the dire state of their economy, and as the value of the rial slides — it has slipped from 80,000 to 800,000 rials to the pound in the space of six years — people are furtively sending money abroad or converting their cash to gold.
The two perspectives are not unconnected.
This underlying economic crisis will be informing the decision-making calculus in Tehran and for all the anxiety abroad, there will be some in government in Iran who are equally nervous about the consequences of escalation.
The regime increasingly finds itself trapped between the diktats of ideology and the realities of power. Less than two years ago, the government’s legitimacy was weakened by the wave of mass protests that swept the country following the brutal murder of Mahsa Jina Amini at the hands of the morality police. It has never fully recovered its authority.
Hawks inside Iran now demand a response to the Damascus attack, as do Iran’s allies in the “axis of resistance” who wonder out loud why Tehran has effectively absented itself from the current struggle against Israel and relied on them as proxies. A credibility gap is growing and it needs to be filled. But how best to do this without causing irrevocable damage to a regime already teetering on the edge of an economic abyss?
One way, of course, is to maintain a credible threat, complicated by ambiguity, which keeps the world guessing and provides Iran with enhanced diplomatic and political leverage.
This is Iran’s performative politics at its best, engaging in a form of psychological operation the country’s leaders have honed so well against dissidents at home. Mixed messaging can serve to discombobulate their opponents — though it is also no doubt a reflection of their own uncertainties.
But such an approach has its limitations too, especially in an atmosphere where the authority of the regime is being challenged both at home and abroad, and where there is a growing sense that Iranian leaders, cornered by their own bombastic rhetoric, are being forced to act in ways that they might prefer to avoid.
This sense of compulsion is unnerving to the regime — and to its enemies. The traditional tendency towards strategic patience, a policy of procrastination which allowed Tehran to defer decisions while keeping everyone guessing, has run out of road.
There is much talk of finding a “goldilocks” solution: an attack that would do enough but no more. But quite how this would be achieved is anybody’s guess.
Amir-Abdollahian has insisted that any strike would be proportionate, precise and importantly avoid the risk of escalation. This has raised the possibility that it would be geographically limited, for instance to the Golan Heights, or that the Iranians would take a series of distinct and contained actions (one option being touted is that Ayatollah Khamenei would take the opportunity to revisit his fatwa against nuclear weapons).
However, the intelligence briefings suggest an assault of an altogether different scale. In the aftermath of the 2020 US drone attack that assassinated Qasem Soleimani, the IRGC general who shaped Tehran’s regional network of allied militias, the Iranians launched missiles against a US base in Iraq, doing more damage than people realised at the time but remaining below the threshold that would have demanded a response by America.
This time around, the current Israeli government, facing its own crisis, is unlikely to err on the side ofcaution in the event of a major escalation. Nor is it likely that the US will be able to stand aside.
The Iranian regime is facing a political conundrum of enormous proportions. Do nothing and it will be mocked at home and abroad as a paper tiger. Do something and it risks rebounding with devastating effect on the Iranian economy and society alike, with consequences for the regime’s stability.
The Islamic Revolution’s 45-year enmity with the state of Israel is coming home to roost. There are choices to be made, and the choices are not good.
Ali Ansari is the director of the Institute of Iranian Studies at the University of St Andrews
author: Ali Ansari

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.title: Chris Packham calls Heineken a ‘vandal’ for cutting down cider orchard
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.subtitle: The brewing giant uprooted trees at Penrhos Orchard in Monmouthshire after a fall in demand for Bulmers cider
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.text:
Chris Packham, the BBC naturalist, has condemned Heineken as an “environmental vandal” for chopping down a 300-acre orchard in south Wales.
Bulmers, the UK’s largest cider maker, which is owned by the Dutch brewing company, uprooted thousands of trees on the Offa’s Dyke path in Monmouthshire after overestimating demand for its drinks. Penrhos Orchard, which was planted in 1997, spanned several large fields and was about the size of 140 football pitches.
Heineken, which plans to sell the land, insisted it had acted in accordance with the Wildlife Act. Packham said that this was “almost irrelevant” when Britain was in the midst of a “biodiversity crisis”.
“What a tragically sad story and a sort of abject shortsightedness,” he said. “They could have offered the land for sale with the trees on it. It could have been turned into a glamping site, a leisure resource, or given to a local community group.”
Packham, the presenter of several TV wildlife series, said that orchards had a special place in British culture but had in recent decades become “an endangered habitat”.
The National Association of Cider Makers said that 2,000 acres of British cider apple orchards had been lost in the past few years which, due to high tannin levels, have no other use than for making the drink. It said that the amount of cider being drunk in the UK had dropped by a third over the past ten years, leading to what it called a “devastating loss of orchards”.
Packham said that those orchards which remain “continue to be a really important resource for wildlife”.
“They produce a lot of blossoms in the spring and in autumn the fallen apples sustain birds and butterflies,” he said.
People in the area said that they were concerned about the effect the felling will have had on migratory bird populations.
Chris Formaggia, an ecologist, said that he had often walked with his children down the footpaths through the orchard, keeping an eye on the various species perched in the trees. He told the BBC the orchard had been “absolutely teeming” with winter thrushes, like fieldfare and redwing, that eat autumn berries before moving on to “wind-blown apple crops”.
“I think inevitably there will be a big loss here, particularly with those wintering populations,” he said. “That foraging and that safety of the trees has gone and it’s not going to be replaced.”
Heineken said that it was “incredibly important that we act responsibly and sustainably at all times” and the move was prompted by the slowing cider market and improved growing practices.
